s10.slug: THURSDAY · 9:36 PM · MISSION STREET, DOWNHILL TO THE HARBOR
body: Mission Street runs downhill to the water the whole way, and at half past nine on a Thursday it belongs to the palms and the Spanish tile and two kids sharing one skateboard. The Borders is dark, a cardboard Dan Brown in the window promising *The Lost Symbol* on Tuesday. The Blockbuster is still open, lit like an aquarium, one clerk inside drifting along the New Releases with a pricing gun. Below it all the harbor lights are strung out on the black, and the air coming up the hill smells of diesel and kelp and the fryer at the fish-and-chips place that closed an hour ago.

She’s a block and a half ahead of him in the brown Justins, walking like she argues, fast and downhill and certain of the ground. The tote bangs on her hip. The cardigan’s on, sleeves pulled down over her hands. Jack has his paper rolled in his fist, red side in. He hasn’t looked at the last page. He hasn’t looked at any of it.

He catches her at Anacapa Street. There isn’t a car in either direction, and she’s standing at the curb waiting for the walk sign — Lena Broussard, who has never in her life waited for a walk sign — with her arms crossed and her face turned toward the harbor.
“You forgot your homework.”
She turns. Her face is wet, all of it, cheekbones to jaw, and she doesn’t wipe it. She looks at the paper in his hand as if she’s never seen it before, and doesn’t take it.
“Bastille was hot,” she says. “I needed air.” Her hand goes to the medal at her throat.
The walk sign comes on, white, ticking, and neither of them crosses.

choices.text: “Okay. Can I walk with you?”
response: She doesn’t answer. She crosses, and on the far side of Anacapa she slows to the speed of somebody who expects company, and that’s the answer. They go down the hill side by side past the Spanish tile and the shut bakery, not talking, and she lets him take the tote off her shoulder.

choices.text: “It’s sixty degrees.”
response: “Then I needed sixty degrees, Costigan.” There’s the edge, the first he’s heard on her all week, and for a second her whole face is almost grateful to have something to put it into. She steps off the curb. He steps off after her.

choices.text: “I hear the harbor’s nice this time of night. Sea lions. Terrible singers. No choruses.”
response: One corner of her mouth gives way, and the laugh gets that far and no farther. “You are a terrible person,” she says, wet-faced, and crosses, and he crosses with her. Down at the bottom of the hill, faint and hoarse, the sea lions are already at it.

s10s.slug: THURSDAY · 10:09 PM · MARISOL HARBOR, THE PIER
body: Mission Street runs downhill to the water the whole way, and Jack goes down it alone with his paper rolled in his fist: past the Borders, dark, a cardboard Dan Brown in the window promising *The Lost Symbol* on Tuesday; past the Blockbuster, lit like an aquarium, one clerk drifting along the New Releases with a pricing gun; past the fish-and-chips place, shut, still breathing fryer oil into the street. Two kids are sharing one skateboard down the middle of the empty road, one riding and one running alongside, trading off at every corner. He walks behind them for three blocks and doesn’t look at the last page. Below it all the harbor lights are strung out on the black. Julian was right. It’s downhill.

The pier starts at the bottom of the hill where Mission runs out of road: wet boards, a chain-link gate propped open with a bait bucket, a hand-lettered sign about not feeding the sea lions that somebody has corrected in marker to NOT FEEDING THEM ENOUGH. He walks out it slower than he walked down the hill. He doesn’t know what he’s going to say, and the pier is long enough to find out he still doesn’t.

He finds her at the very end, past the bait shack with its grille pulled down over a hand-painted squid and the fish market’s dark windows, out where the railing stops at a chain, under the one lamp. She’s standing with her arms crossed and her face to the breakwater. When the boards tell her somebody’s coming she turns around, and her face is wet, all of it, cheekbones to jaw, and she doesn’t wipe it.

She looks at the paper in his hand as if she’s never seen it before. “Bastille was hot,” she says, before he’s asked her anything. “I needed air.” Her hand goes to the medal at her throat, and she looks at him as if waiting to see whether he’ll buy it.

choices.text: Stand next to her at the chain. Don’t ask.
response: He comes and stands beside her at the chain, close enough to count, not close enough to be a question. She looks at him sidelong, once, and then back out at the breakwater, and after a while her shoulder settles an inch his way.

choices.text: “You forgot your homework.”
response: “I didn’t forget it,” she says. “I abandoned it. There’s a difference, and it’s moral.” It’s the first thing all week that sounds like her. She takes the paper out of his hand, looks at it, and gives it straight back.

choices.text: “Julian said this is where people come.”
response: “Julian should mind his business,” she says. “Julian should finish his song.” She hears it land, and her mouth twists. “That was mean. He’s good. He’s very good.” She turns back to the water. “That’s the problem.”

s10b.slug: THURSDAY · 10:18 PM · MARISOL HARBOR, THE END OF THE PIER

body.text: They walk out the pier together, past the bait shack with its grille pulled down over a hand-painted squid, past the fish market’s dark windows and a hose coiled on the wet boards, out to where the planks go gray and soft underfoot and the railing stops at a chain. She stays half a step ahead, as she has all the way down Mission, but not so far ahead that it counts.
body.else: So they stand at the chain a while, side by side, the planks shifting under them on the swell.

body: Down on the float the sea lions are stacked three deep, barking at something nobody else can see; every so often one slides off with a slap and swims a lap and hauls itself back up into the pile and gets barked at for its trouble. Out past the breakwater a bell buoy rings now and then on the swell.

Across the harbor the Anchor sits on its wharf with the counter lit and the kitchen dark. From here Jack can see the glow of the pie case and a shape at the register that’s Gloria, and a sheet of paper taped inside the door that he can’t read at this distance and doesn’t need to: CLOSED FOR CLEANING — PIE & COFFEE ONLY. Once a year the hood men come with their tarps and their degreaser, and the Hobart sits cold, and six hours at eight dollars go wherever money goes when you don’t make it.
“That’s my night off,” he says, and points.

body.text: She looks across the water at his dark kitchen. “Your night off,” she says, “and you spent it at an open mic and then chasing a girl down Mission Street. Costigan, that is the saddest thing I have ever heard, and I’ve been to a Vigil Mass in Metairie with a guitar choir.”
body.else: She looks across the water at his dark kitchen. “Your night off,” she says, “and you spent it at an open mic and then hunting a girl down to the end of a pier. Costigan, that is the saddest thing I have ever heard, and I’ve been to a Vigil Mass in Metairie with a guitar choir.”

body: “How much is a night off?” “Forty-eight dollars. Plus the tip share.” She does the arithmetic with her eyes on the far side of the harbor; he can watch her do it. “What were you going to do with forty-eight dollars, Costigan?” “Books,” he says. It’s true as far as it goes. She looks at him sidelong, and lets it go exactly that far. “Books,” she says. “Lord. You’re worse than me.”

Then she sits down on the very end of the pier, where there’s no rail, and pulls off the Justins one and then the other and sets them side by side on the planks behind her, toes even. She puts her legs over the drop. Her bare feet hang over black water, fifteen feet of nothing under her heels, and the swell comes in under the pier and lifts and sucks at the pilings, and she swings her feet once, as if it’s her daddy’s porch.

Jack sits down beside her with his own legs over the edge, because it would be stranger not to. He wants her six inches farther back. He wants it badly and all at once — fifteen feet, the tide running under the boards, and he’s a Mill Creek Park kid who grew up on stories about Lake Glacier taking somebody’s cousin every March. He doesn’t say it. She isn’t his to say it to.
She catches him looking at the drop anyway. “I can swim, Costigan,” she says. “I grew up below sea level. We learn before we walk.”
His hands want a cigarette. They’ve wanted one since the second chorus. The pack is in the inside pocket of the Carhartt, against his ribs, and his hands know exactly where.

choices.text: Light one.
choices.key: Lena smoked half of your cigarette, then put it in the tin.
response: He lights it with his back to the wind and gets one pull before she reaches over without looking and takes it out of his mouth, as she has every time since a porch on Seacliff Road. He waits for the stub on the planks. Instead she looks at it, and then she puts it to her own mouth, where his just was, and drags.

She coughs like a girl from a Catholic school — bent over her knees, eyes streaming, a hand flat on the wet boards. “Lord have *mercy*. You pay money for this.” Then she takes a second one, slow, better, looking across the water at the Anchor, and lets the smoke go out over the harbor. The coal lights her face orange from underneath. The filter’s damp from his mouth and then from hers. Jack watches her mouth on his cigarette and wants her, plainly. There’s a grain of tobacco on her lower lip that she doesn’t know about. She takes a third drag, short, and looks at the coal as if it has told her something.

She stubs it out on the plank between them, carefully, and blows on it to be sure, and takes the tin out of her cardigan pocket. She tears a corner off the Bastille receipt in her tote and writes on her knee.

response.title: A slip of paper, folded into the tin
response.text: No. 3 · 9/10/09 · the harbor · confiscated and partially consumed by the Reliquarian. Do not ask.
“Fourth-class,” she says, and snaps the lid. “I founded it. I can amend it.”

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. Do not ask.

choices.text: Sit on your hands.
choices.key: You didn’t smoke at the end of the pier.
response: He sits on them — actually sits on them, palms down on the wet planks under his thighs, like an altar boy who’s been warned. The pack stays where it is. She notices. She notices anything that has his hands in it.
“You’re not smoking.” “Not tonight.” She’s quiet a while, her feet going over the dark. Then she knocks his boot with her bare heel, once. “Good.”

choices.text: Hand her the pack. “Hold these. I’m weak tonight.”
choices.key: You gave Lena your cigarettes to hold.
response: She weighs the pack in her palm, unimpressed. “That’s not how this works, Costigan. I collect them one at a time, off your face.” Then she tucks it into her cardigan pocket anyway, where it knocks once against the tin, and keeps her hand over the pocket.

s10c.slug: THURSDAY · 10:41 PM · MARISOL HARBOR, THE END OF THE PIER
body: She takes the Hopkins out of his back pocket as if it were hers. He’s caught her reading his margins since the first week, upside down across the seminar table, and tonight she doesn’t bother waiting for him to look away. She just reaches behind him and takes it, and the book falls open where it falls open now, at the Benedict holy card, at the sonnet he’s read so many times the page has gone soft as a dish towel.

Under the lamp he can see what she sees. The Latin from Jeremiah at the top. The poem. And in the margin beside the first line, small, in his own pencil, from a night last week he would very much like back: *Show Lena.*
She looks at her own name. Then she tilts the page to the lamp and reads it aloud, in the voice she uses at Hale’s table, the one that makes Caleb sit up, every stress where Hopkins hammered it in:
*“Thou art indeed just, Lord, if I contend / With thee; but, sir, so what I plead is just. / Why do sinners’ ways prosper? and why must / Disappointment all I endeavour end?”*
Her voice holds through the sinners. It goes, a little, on *friend*:
*“Wert thou my enemy, O thou my friend, / How wouldst thou worse, I wonder, than thou dost / Defeat, thwart me?”*

She stops there. The sea lions start up and quit. She reads the rest to herself with her lips moving — the banks and brakes, the birds building, *Time’s eunuch* — and then, after a silence long enough that he thinks she’s finished, the last line out loud, quieter, as though it belongs to her now:
*“Mine, O thou lord of life, send my roots rain.”*

She closes the book on her thumb and turns it over and finds the purple stamp along the edges of the pages, CARDINAL MOONEY H.S. LIBRARY — DISCARD. “They threw out Hopkins.” “They threw out a lot. I got Augustine for a dime and Hopkins for a quarter.” “Hopkins cost more than Augustine?” “Hopkins was in better shape.” That gets the corner of her mouth, a little. Then she opens the book again to the holy card and the pencil in the margin. “*Show Lena*,” she reads. “Well.” She puts the book back in his hands. “You did.”

body.text: In her cardigan pocket his pack of Reds rides against the tin.

body: “Do you ever yell at Him?” she asks. She’s looking at the dark kitchen across the water, not at him.
Jack thinks about saying no.

choices.text: “Once. When I was sixteen.”
response: “Once,” he says. “Sixteen.” The swell goes in under the pier and comes back out. “It wasn’t yelling, really. It was more like finding out somebody was in the room.” That’s where the sentence ends, and he lets it. She doesn’t ask him for the rest. She nods, slowly, and turns it over, and gives him back the quiet.

choices.text: “Only during Browns games. He knows what He did.”
response: She snorts — actually snorts, Lena Broussard, at the end of a pier — and she lets him have the dodge. He watches her decide to. She looks back across the harbor, and the swell goes in under the pier and comes back out.

choices.text: “Do you?”
response: She takes that as fair. She takes it, he thinks, as permission. “Yes,” she says.

s10c2.slug: THURSDAY · 10:49 PM · MARISOL HARBOR, THE END OF THE PIER
body: Then she tells him.

“My grandmother died in the storm,” she says. “In ’05. Grandmère. Lucille Guidry. Five foot nothing in her church shoes. She taught me gumbo standing on a step stool at her stove, and she had hands like an oyster shucker’s, all knuckle, and she said the rosary in Cajun French so fast you’d think she was mad at the Blessed Mother. She wasn’t. She just wanted to get to the end and start over.” She draws a breath, and it shakes, and she flattens it. “Water. Heat. Four days.”
He opens his mouth — he doesn’t know for what — and she gets there first.

“It doesn’t matter how.” She says it fast and level, worn smooth, a sentence she has said to herself more often than to anyone else. “We didn’t get to bury her till November. In the good dress.” A flicker, there and gone, of the girl who wins: “She’d have killed us otherwise.” He heard her say it once before, on the first Sunday, about a senator — *you bury everybody, and you bury them in the good dress* — and he took it for a figure of speech.

“The medal came back to my mother in a plastic bag,” she says. “In February. And my mother put it in my hand when I turned fifteen and didn’t say a word. She closed my fingers on it and went back in the kitchen. And I have never asked her one question. Not one.” She shakes her head. “I argue with *everybody*, Costigan. I argued a parking officer out of a ticket the day I got here.” He knows. He watched her do it from across the Commons Lawn, a pelican lamp under her arm, before he knew her name. “And I have never asked my mother one question.” Her hand finds the medal and holds it.

“The year after, I yelled at Him. I was fourteen. I went to Mass every single morning for a year — wherever we were living, whatever church had its roof back, with the old ladies and their plastic rain bonnets — so He’d have to look at me. I’d kneel there and think, *look at me. Look at what You did.*” She lifts one shoulder. “And somewhere in there — I couldn’t tell you what month — it stopped being a fight. And I kept going anyway.”

choices.text: Say nothing. Let the quiet be hers.
response: He lets the quiet be hers. The sea lions sort something out among themselves on the float; a halyard pings against a mast somewhere in the dark. After a while she breathes out, long, and swings her feet once over the water, and her shoulders come down an inch.

choices.text: “Tell me about the gumbo.”

Tomatoes are for Creoles and Yankees.” The Banks Street speed comes back into it for a sentence, and he’s so glad to hear it he could put his head down on the planks. “She’d smack your hand with the spoon.” She wipes her face with the cardigan cuff, finally. “I make it. I make it wrong. Every time, it’s wrong in the same place.”

s10c3.slug: THURSDAY · 10:58 PM · MARISOL HARBOR, THE END OF THE PIER
body: She holds her hand out for his paper. He gives it to her, and the red pen with it. She pages past her own few marks — a single *No.* on the first page, a bracketed *source?* on the second, not much else, not this week — to the last page, and holds it under the lamp for him.

body.title: Red ink, last page
body.text: *You keep writing “we” when you mean “I.” Who are you paying for, Costigan?*
“Monday, on the beach, you said ‘family stuff. Mostly.’ I let you have ‘mostly.’” She taps the page with the cap of the red pen. “I want it back.”
And then, gentler: “You told me your daddy’s good. Is he?”

body: She waits. Her bare feet hang over the water. Across the harbor the pie case glows in the dark diner like a votive rack.

choices.text: Tell her about Danny.
choices.key: You told Lena your brother is in prison.
response: “My brother,” he says. He gives her the sentences he gave Theo on Monday morning, in the same order, because they’re the ones he has. Trumbull Correctional, a state prison outside Warren, half an hour from the house. Five years. A fight; a guy got hurt bad. He pleaded. Three more to go, maybe less. “He gets one book a month. From me. Used. I erase the margins first, because they can’t have writing in them, and I send what I wrote on a separate sheet.”

She doesn’t ask what the fight was. Of everyone he’s ever met, she might be the one who knows best how not to ask a thing. What she asks is, “What’s his name?” “Danny.” “Danny,” she says, once, carefully, as if she means to bring it to Mass in the morning.

Then she does the thing she does, which is make it an argument, and the argument is mercy. She puts his paper back in his hands, last page up. “Then you can love him. You can’t pay for anybody, Costigan. You wrote it yourself, in twelve-point Times: there’s one who pays, and it isn’t you. Read your own paper.”

response.text: He looks at the dark kitchen across the water. “He’s not good,” he says. “My dad. He’s in the garage. He goes out there after supper and sits with the radio on, and the truck’s in the driveway with nowhere to be.” She leans over until her shoulder is against his arm, and leaves it there.

choices.text: “My brother. I can’t yet.”
choices.key: You told Lena there’s a brother you can’t talk about yet.
response: “My brother,” he says, and gets that far, and finds the rest of it isn’t there to say. “I can’t yet.” She studies him under the lamp. Then she nods. “Okay. When you can.” She folds the paper with the red page inside and puts it back in his hands.

response.text: “He’s — ” He hears it coming and can’t get out of its way. “Mostly.” She laughs at that — at the word she just took back from him, thrown back at her across a pier at eleven at night — and finally wipes her face with the heel of her hand.
“He’s okay,” Jack says, which isn’t an answer, and she lets it not be one.

choices.text: Tell her a Danny story instead — the funny one.
choices.key: You told Lena about Danny and the frozen lake, and not the rest.
response: So he tells her about Danny without telling her about Danny. The winter Danny was eighteen and Jack was fourteen, Danny took the Silverado down to Lake Glacier in Mill Creek Park when the ice was a foot thick, put Jack behind the wheel, told him the brake was more of a suggestion, and the two of them did doughnuts in the dark until the trees went around them in the headlights like a carousel. Frank found out on Monday because a park ranger knew the truck — forest green, rust over the wheel wells, St. Christopher on the visor, the only one like it in Mahoning County. Frank stood in the garage and said, “God help the both of you,” and grounded Danny, who was eighteen and technically couldn’t be grounded, and Danny stayed grounded anyway, for a month, out of respect.

She laughs, finally, all the way, out over the water, one hand flat on the boards to keep herself on the pier. Then she looks at him, and the laugh goes quiet without going away. “You love him.” “Yeah.” She can tell there’s more. It’s right there in her face that she can tell. She lets it be.

response.text: “Don’t ask me about my dad tonight,” he says, and she nods, and wipes her face with the heel of her hand.

choices.text: “Everybody. That’s the joke.”
choices.key: You told Lena you were paying for everybody.
response: “Everybody,” he says. “That’s the joke. I’m Catholic, Broussard. We pay for everybody. It’s in the brochure.” She looks at him under the lamp, long enough that he has to look at the water instead. Then she allows it, and folds the page closed.

response.text: “And my dad’s good,” he says. She leaves him that word, too, the second time she’s had to, and hands him back his paper.

s10d.slug: FRIDAY · 12:29 AM · THE WHARF BUS STOP, THEN OCEAN ROAD
body: At 12:29 the last 11 is idling at the wharf stop with its windows lit and its doors folded open and one passenger asleep against the glass, a man in a fish-plant apron with his cap over his eyes. The driver looks at them. Jack has a foot on the step.

Lena stands on the curb with her boots in one hand and looks at the bus: the bright aisle, the yellow grab bars, the placard for a personal-injury lawyer running the length of the windows. “I don’t want to be in a lit box with people,” she says. The driver gives them a polite few seconds more. Jack takes his foot back off the step. The doors fold shut and the 11 pulls away up Mission with its one sleeper, and the wharf is very quiet. He would have gotten on.

So it’s three miles. Ocean Road climbs out of town along the bluff, and while they were on the pier the fog came in off the water and filled the road to the tops of the streetlights, so each one stands in its own gray room. Eucalyptus on the inland side, dripping: the menthol smell, and under it, rain that hasn’t happened yet. A sprinkler ticking on somebody’s lawn at a quarter to one. The taquería at the edge of town shut, its chairs upside down on its tables. A raccoon walks the top of a fence beside them for half a block and drops off the far side.

She walks the first mile barefoot on the sidewalk with the Justins hooked in one hand. “Your feet,” he says, at a broken bottle glittering under a streetlight. “Are from Louisiana,” she says, stepping around it. “They’ve been through worse than California.” Where the sidewalk gives out to gravel shoulder she sits on the guardrail and pulls them back on and stamps her heels down into them, and they go on.

She’s cold. Her arms are crossed, her hands up inside the cardigan sleeves, and out on the open stretch, where the wind comes straight up the bluff off the water, her shoulders rise toward her ears. Jack takes off the Carhartt and puts it around her.

It’s enormous on her. It comes down to the middle of her thighs, and it smells of cigarettes and the Hobart’s steam and him, and the collar has folded under at the back. He fixes it, his hands at her neck in the fog for exactly as long as it takes to fix a collar, his knuckles against the warm skin under her jaw, and then he takes his hands back and puts them in the pockets of his jeans, and it is the most expensive thing he’s done all night.

body.text: “It’s his,” Jack says. She pulls it closed in front of her with both fists and is quiet for a hundred yards.
body.else: “You know this is too big on you, too,” she says, from somewhere inside it. He knows.

body: For a while the road is only the road. Then, out of nowhere: “What would you be doing right now? If you weren’t off.” “Racks,” he says. “The late rush. Fishermen and drunks. Rudy does eggs for people who won’t remember eating them, and I wash the plates.” “And the waitress with the pencil in her hair. From August.” “Gloria.” So he tells her about Gloria: the bus tub on her hip, the pie case, the two chalkboards by the register, and what it says on the second one. Lena stops dead on the gravel shoulder. “She makes you rate the pie.” “In public.” “What did you give the marionberry?” “Four.” “*Four.*” She says it the way a nun says *divorce*. “A woman bakes you a pie with her own two hands and you give her a four. In *chalk*.” “It was a four.” “There is no such thing as a four. A pie is a seven or it’s a declaration of war.” “Then it was a declaration of war.” She walks on, shaking her head inside his collar, and he has the feeling he’s going to hear about the four again.

Farther on, where the bluff drops away and the surf is right there under the guardrail, he asks her about home. “Dupre Street,” she says. “Mid-City. A shotgun my daddy and his brothers put back together with their own hands, two years of weekends.” Four and a half feet of water; the line’s still on the shed, she says, because her daddy won’t paint over it. The whole season the Saints had no home — San Antonio, Baton Rouge, the Meadowlands — her daddy, who has had season tickets since 1981, drove in every Sunday from wherever they were living and sat on the porch of the gutted house on a folding chair with a radio, because the living room was studs and wet sheetrock, and listened to them lose. “Three and thirteen,” she says. She pulls the jacket tighter. “He says it was the best season he ever had.”

Half a mile on she says, “He called early. Before Bastille. I told him I was fine.” A car comes by slow in the fog, headlights first and then a red smear and then nothing. “I’m extremely good at fine.”
There it is, standing open in the middle of Ocean Road: *Are you, though. Does he know. What does he say when you tell him that.*

choices.text: Say nothing. Keep walking.
response: Jack walks right past it. He keeps his hands in his pockets and his eyes on the white line and his mouth shut, and the silence is so loud to him he’s sure she can hear it over the surf.

choices.text: “Does he know you’re not?”
response: She takes three steps before she answers. “He knows what I tell him,” she says. “That’s how it works from two thousand miles. You tell each other the parts that travel.” She pulls the jacket tighter. “He’s good, Costigan. He’s a good man. Don’t.”

choices.text: “You don’t have to be fine with me.”
response: She walks ten steps before she answers. “I know,” she says, with her chin down. Then, because she’s Lena and it’s one in the morning: “Don’t let it go to your head, Youngstown.”

s10d2.slug: FRIDAY · 1:04 AM · OCEAN ROAD, THE OPEN STRETCH
body: So they argue instead, because they can, and the argument runs backward. It’s one in the morning and the fog is beading in her hair. “Aquinas didn’t get me to the early Mass, Costigan. Being furious did. If I’d been reasonable I’d have stayed in bed.” And Jack, of all people, hears himself defending reason — defending Job’s friends.

“They came and sat on the ground with him,” he says. “Seven days and seven nights, and nobody said a word, because they saw his grief was very great. That’s the best part of the book. They were perfect. They were perfect right up until they opened their mouths.” “So your argument for reason is three men who should have stayed quiet.” “My argument is that showing up is reason. Sitting in the dirt with a guy is — ”

“And you skipped the ending.” She doesn’t let him have the dash. “Forty-two, verse seven. God finally shows up, and He tells the friends they were *wrong*. Job yelled at Him for most of the book, and Job’s the one who spoke rightly. The yeller wins, Costigan. Aquinas wrote a whole commentary on it — he reads it like a disputation, and God *likes* the argument.” The road bends, and the campus lights show through the fog far ahead, smeared and orange. He doesn’t have the rest of his sentence, and he isn’t going to get it now. She walks along beside him with her fists in his jacket, having won, and waits to see what he’ll do about it.

choices.text: “Job got a whirlwind. You got a school bus from Minnesota.”
response: It reaches her a step late. Then she laughs out loud on Ocean Road at one in the morning, a big helpless Gulf Coast honk of a laugh that stops her in her tracks — she has to bend over with her hands on her knees in the middle of the empty road, in his jacket, to get to the end of it — and he stands there in the fog in his flannel and gets to hear the whole thing. “Oh, that’s *awful*,” she says, straightening up, wiping her eyes with his sleeve. “That’s sacrilege. They were *Catholics*, Costigan. They had a priest who’d never seen a crawfish.” She starts walking again. “He held one up like a relic.”

choices.text: “Nobody yells at an empty room.”
response: She stops walking. In the fog, in his jacket, in the middle of Ocean Road, she turns around and looks at him. “Say that again.” He says it again. She stands there with it. Then she starts walking, a little faster than before, with her hands jammed deep in his jacket pockets.

choices.text: “Ask her one question. Your mother. Just one.”
choices.key: You told Lena to ask her mother one question.
response: Her chin comes up, and for a second he thinks he’s about to get the full Broussard, three subpoints and a rebuttal. “Not tonight, Costigan.” They walk. There are no blocks out here, only guardrail and eucalyptus and the surf down below, but they go about a block’s worth of fog before she says, mostly into his collar, “…Maybe at Thanksgiving.”

s10e.slug: FRIDAY · 2:08 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: Delgado at 2:08 is a concrete grid in the fog with a dozen windows lit for no good reason. Through the lobby glass Marcus is asleep at the front desk, head tipped back, mouth open, a calculus textbook face down on his chest going up and down. Neither of them goes in. Lena sits on the front steps in the jacket, and Jack sits beside her with a foot of cold concrete between them.

At 2:10 a horn sounds down on the bluff — two long, one short, one long — and then the freight itself, more a feeling in the steps than a sound. Jack starts counting under his breath. He’s counted trains since he was six, lying awake on Glenwood Avenue with the window cracked, listening to the freights cross the South Side in the dark.

“What are you doing?” “Counting.” “Counting what?” “Cars. I do it when I can’t sleep.” “You’re not trying to sleep. You’re on a step.” “I’m not really trying to count, either.” She listens. Then she counts too, out loud, a half beat behind him and then not behind him at all, the two of them going up through the thirties and the forties in whispers on the front steps of Delgado Hall while Marcus sleeps on the other side of the glass.

The last car goes by and the sound pulls away up the coast, and the bluff is quiet again. “Sixty-three,” Jack says. “Sixty-five.” “It was sixty-three.” “Sixty-five, Costigan. There were two engines.” “Engines aren’t cars.” “They *pull* the cars. They’re the most important cars.” “That’s like counting the priest in the attendance.” “He *is* in the attendance. He’s the first one there. Without him it’s just people in a room.”

“Why do you count?” He thinks about the window on Glenwood Avenue, cracked an inch in every weather. “When I was six my dad worked second shift. Home around one. There was a freight across the South Side at about a quarter to, and when I got to the end of it, his truck would be in the drive.” “And if it wasn’t?” “Then I counted the next one.” She’s quiet after that.

“My daddy gets up at three,” she says. “For the boats. The screen door, and then the truck. I used to lie there and wait for the truck to start so I could go back to sleep.” She looks off down the dark toward the tracks. “We’re a very boring kind of people, Costigan. People who listen for trucks.”
She tucks her chin down inside the Carhartt’s collar. “I’ll bring it back,” she says. “I’m warm for the first time since Monday.”

body.text: “And you sat down at Bastille and didn’t ask what I was marking,” she says. “I noticed.”
“And you let me have my table tonight,” she says. “At Bastille. I noticed.”
“And the cortado,” she says. “I noticed.”

body: Then she turns her head and looks at him, and all the New Orleans goes out of her voice — the speed and the theater and the saints — and what’s left is a girl on a step at two in the morning who means it. “Thank you, Jack.”
She’s said his name before. Not like that.

choices.text: “Goodnight, Magdalena.”
choices.key: You called her Magdalena, and she let you.
response: Her mother, the Holy Ghost, and Laney when she wants something: she told him the rule on a porch the first night, and he hasn’t used the name since. She doesn’t correct him. She looks at him in the fog with her chin in his collar, and then she stands up and brushes off the back of his jacket and goes up the last step.

choices.text: “Text me when you get upstairs.”
response: “It’s one flight, Costigan.” “Text me.” She looks at him as if he’s said something in a language she almost speaks. He doesn’t explain what it means where he comes from. She doesn’t ask. She stands up and brushes off the back of his jacket.

choices.text: “Goodnight, Broussard.” Let her go in first.
response: “Goodnight, Costigan.” The old names, handed back and forth across a step at two in the morning like a tool that still works. She stands. He stays where he is and lets her have the door.

s10f.slug: FRIDAY · 2:16 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: Through the glass she crosses the lobby in Danny’s jacket, the hem swinging at her thighs, her boots quiet on the linoleum, past Marcus and his calculus rising and falling. At the elevator she pushes the button and stands with her back to the glass, small inside the Carhartt. The doors open on their yellow light. She gets in. The doors close, and the numbers over them go to 2 and stay there.
Jack sits on the steps in his flannel. The fog has gotten into it; when he rubs his arms his palms come away damp. Without the Carhartt the cold finds every place it used to be, and he lets it.

body.text: I’m there. Go to sleep, Youngstown. —L.
she just walked in wearing ur jacket. not asking. thank u FIREMAN. xo

body: He doesn’t go up. He sits on the step while the fog comes down over the lawn and puts out the path lamps one after another, until the Lagoon is gone and the Grove is gone and there’s only the lit lobby at his back and Marcus breathing over his calculus, and somewhere up the coast, too far off now to hear, the freight going on north with nobody counting it.

s11.slug: FRIDAY · 2:30 PM · DRIFTWOOD BOOKS, MISSION STREET
body: At two on Friday the sun has burned through, and the Anacapa lot is glare and gull droppings and hot asphalt. Jack stops behind Kevin’s Odyssey because there’s no way not to. Across the back glass, in the white polish, it says WHO DAT, and then the 6 has been wiped out with a thumb, and then a 5, a 4 and a 3, each one written and each one struck through with a single hard white line, and then, big and fresh, 2 DAYS. Caught up all at once, sometime this morning, by somebody in a hurry to be current again.

Theo is leaning on the SL two spaces down with the keys hooked on one finger. “She came down at seven with the shoe polish,” he says. “In your jacket.” He was out here at seven moving the car ahead of the parking people. He doesn’t ask about the jacket. He never asks.

The SL goes down Mission with the top down and *Brideshead* in Jack’s lap, every margin of it blank. He did it Wednesday night with a Pink Pearl, one page at a time, until his whole running fight with Evelyn Waugh lay on the desk in gray crumbs. Danny can’t have writing. Danny gets the book clean, and the notes on a separate sheet.

Driftwood smells of old paper and cat. Boethius and Mrs. Danvers are asleep on the register in one heap, and it’s impossible to say where either cat stops. The owner looks up over the reading glasses on her beaded chain, and when Jack tells her where the book is going she doesn’t blink. She ships books to prisons as the seller, “because the prisons only take books from sellers” — said like someone who has won that argument with a mailroom — and has for years, for a woman whose son is at Soledad. She slides the *Brideshead* into a mailer of her own, copies the Trumbull address off Jack’s index card in square capitals, and sets it on a scale with a brass pan. Media mail. “Two thirty-eight.” “And the mailer?” “The mailer’s on me.” He counts it out of the last of Tuesday’s tips, two singles and change, onto the counter between the cats.

Theo comes out of the back with a book and puts it in Jack’s hands: Everyman’s Library, *Brideshead Revisited*, bound in cloth, a ribbon marker sewn into the spine, an edition made to outlast whoever reads it. He pays with a bill folded in half and doesn’t wait for change. “Not on the tab,” he says. At home the Post-it is still on the espresso machine in Theo’s neat hand, *+ 1 MALIBU —T.V.*, open. Jack doesn’t argue.

The post office is across the street, and the flag out front is at half-staff, hanging straight down in the windless afternoon. Nobody has to tell him why. Inside he buys a forty-four-cent stamp for the letter he wrote this morning at four, after he gave up on sleep.

body.text: *Write him. Even when there’s nothing to say.* The letter is mostly nothing to say. He wrote it anyway, because a man with a rosary on his wrist told him to over a flattop on Tuesday night.

body.title: Folded in thirds, to Trumbull
body.text:
Danny —

Describe it, you said. Okay. Sixty-six degrees. Green at the top of the waves and gray underneath. It sounds like a truck going by that never finishes going by. The fog comes in at night like it’s got somewhere to be.

I told the veil girl about you. She didn’t ask what. She asked your name.

Next month you get Hopkins. He yells at God in sonnets. You’ll like him.

—the Professor

body: Back in the SL, Theo doesn’t start the car. He’s looking at the flag. “Where were you?” he says. “Eight years ago.”

“Fifth grade. St. Brigid’s.” Sister Rose wheeled the TV cart in after the second plane and didn’t turn it off, and nobody did fractions that day. Jack’s mother came down from the school office and stood at the back of the room with her hand on the radiator, a month from Rosie. “When we got home my dad’s truck was in the driveway. Nobody sent him home from Lordstown. He just came home, at noon, and sat in the truck with the radio on. He was still sitting there at three.”

Theo nods. “My parents were still married,” he says, as if giving a date. “My father was at the Toronto film festival. They grounded everything. He and two other producers rented a Lincoln and drove home to Los Angeles. Four days.” He puts the key in the ignition and doesn’t turn it. “Longest he’s ever stayed anywhere.”

choices.text: “Thanks for not asking. About the jacket. About any of it.”
response: Theo looks at the flag a little longer, and then at the cloth book in Jack’s lap, and not at Jack. When he talks it’s short. “I’m not good at much, Costigan. I’m good at not asking.” He starts the car.
choices.key: You thanked Theo for not asking.

journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him Friday, media mail through Driftwood, margins erased; the ocean went in a letter. Lena knows. She asked his name.

body: St. Brendan’s courtyard at three-twenty-five on a Saturday is empty except for the olive tree and Fr. Osei, who is on his knees in the flower bed in a black clerical shirt with the sleeves rolled and a pair of rubber boots, losing to the sprinkler. Out of his office window comes his father’s record, the one Jack heard over the chessboard, loud enough to carry across the courtyard. The sprinkler head is hissing sideways. Osei has a wrench on it. Every time he tightens it, it finds a new direction, and the newest direction is his face.
On the board by the Newman house door, in Mrs. Fitch’s hand: CONFESSIONS SATURDAY 3:30–4:45 · WEDNESDAY 8:00 · OR WHENEVER YOU KNOCK.

Jack is here because an eighty-four-year-old woman on Glenwood Avenue, with EWTN on in the next room, told him *Go next week*. He walked the long way around the Grove to leave room to change his mind, changed it twice, and came anyway.

Osei sits back on his heels, wipes his face with his sleeve, and looks up with water in his beard and the pleasure of an excuse. “Jack. You have come to knock?” He gestures with the wrench at the sprinkler, which hisses at both of them. “Or to watch a doctor lose to a sprinkler?” Last time it was the box or the board, and Jack took the board and was mated in four. Osei remembers; it’s in his face.

“My nonna said go next week,” Jack says. “It’s next week.” Osei’s eyebrows climb, slowly, all the way. “A grandmother,” he says, “is not an opinion. She is a diagnosis.” He checks the watch on his wet wrist. “I open at three-thirty. You have five minutes to decide if you are a penitent or a plumber.”

choices.text: Knock.
choices.key: You went to confession, like Nonna said.
response: Osei gets up with the olive tree for a handrail, the left leg brought along after, and squelches across the flagstones to the converted coat closet with KNOCK (gently) on the door. After a minute: “Come.” Lemon polish over old wool; a kneeler and a folding chair, so you can choose; a linen screen with a lamp behind it. Jack takes the kneeler. On the other side the rubber boots creak.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned.” He says how long it’s been. He says what he came to say. It takes longer than he planned.

When he’s finished, Osei is quiet a while. Then he says — and it could be said to anyone who ever knelt there — “In the hospital, the patients who would not let the nurses lift them were always the ones who tore something.” The lamp hums behind the linen. “Letting yourself be lifted is also humility.” For a penance: “Call your grandmother and tell her you went. And a decade.” Jack says the Act of Contrition. On the linen the shadow of a hand lifts. “God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” “Amen.”

Outside, Jack sits on the bench under the olive tree, damp from the sprinkler, and opens the RAZR. It’s ten to seven on Glenwood Avenue. Nonna picks up with EWTN going behind her, and he tells her he went. The line is quiet, full of her breathing. “Bravo, Giacomino,” she says. “*Bravo.*” Thirty seconds, start to finish, and she hangs up on herself, the receiver clattering into its cradle on the nightstand. He sits with the closed phone in his hand and the decade still to say, and starts it.

choices.text: Help him with the sprinkler instead.
choices.key: You helped Fr. Osei lose to his sprinkler instead of going to confession.
response: “Give me the wrench.” Jack kneels in the wet bed beside him, and for five minutes they bring a medical degree and a third of a philosophy education to bear on a brass sprinkler head from 1962 and fix nothing. It gets Jack in the ear and Osei down the collar. At one point it stops dead, and they both sit back in triumph, and it comes on again full blast and soaks them to the skin. Osei ends up flat on his back on the flagstones under the olive tree, boots in the marigolds, laughing from the belly. “The box will keep,” he says, without lifting his head. “Grandmothers do not.”

Then he gets up, wrings out his sleeve, limps off to the closet at three-thirty on the dot, and leaves the door ajar. Jack stays with the sprinkler. A grad student knocks, goes in, and comes out walking differently. Mrs. Fitch sets a lemon bar on a napkin by his knee and goes back inside. At a quarter to five the closet door closes, gently, from the inside, and Jack is still kneeling in the mud with the wrench in his hand.

choices.text: Ask about the limp.
choices.key: You asked Fr. Osei about his limp, and didn’t knock.
response: “Does it hurt? The leg.” Osei doesn’t answer right away. His eyes go, not to Jack’s face, but to Jack’s left eyebrow, to the scar, friendly and professional, the look of the man who once told him it was a ring, or a tooth. “You tell me yours, one day,” he says, “and I’ll tell you mine.” He hands Jack the wrench and squelches off toward the closet. At the door he turns. “The door is open till quarter to five.”

At four o’clock Jack sets the wrench on the bench and goes and stands at the closet door. KNOCK (gently). He lifts his hand. He stands there with it up, close enough to see the brush marks in the varnish, and on the other side a man is waiting, as patiently as he waited at the chessboard. Jack puts the hand in his pocket. He walks out to Ocean Road with rust from the wrench still on his fingers and waits for the bus, and when it comes he gets on.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Asked about the leg: “You tell me yours, one day, and I’ll tell you mine.”

body: Jack’s first Saturday at the Anchor is a different animal from a Tuesday. By eleven the booths are full of Las Olas kids sobering up on hash browns, two fishermen at the counter are eating pie with the slow seriousness of men who get up at four, and Rudy is on the line flipping eggs for people who will not remember eating them. Somebody keeps feeding the jukebox Patsy Cline, and Gloria keeps letting them.
At a quarter to nine the RAZR went in his apron pocket, and he read it with wet hands at the back door.

Out front the chalkboard says PIE OF THE DAY: OLALLIEBERRY, and at half past eleven Gloria comes through the swinging door with a fork and a sliver on a saucer and holds both out at him until he dries his hands. “Hon. You rated my marionberry a four in front of God and the register. You’re gonna rate this one.”

He eats it standing at the Hobart: nearly black, tart and then not, the crust shattering the right way. He takes a second bite to be sure, which is a mistake, because now he’s sure. “Nine.” Gloria waits. “Dad would eat two pieces and complain about the second.” Gloria nods as if that is precisely the kind of thing a person should say about a pie, and goes out and chalks it on the board under the marionberry.

PIE OF THE DAY: OLALLIEBERRY
JACK’S RATINGS:
MARIONBERRY 4/10
OLALLIEBERRY 9/10

body: At 11:48 the last-but-one 11 bus sighs at the wharf stop, and through the window over the Hobart he sees who gets off it. Then the bell over the front door, and Gloria’s voice: “Dish man. You got a visitor.”

Lena is just inside the door in Keds and a sundress and the cardigan, his jacket folded over her arm — Danny’s Carhartt, the canvas pale at the seams. She’s looking at the back booth, where in August she saw a magazine on a table and walked out. Then she stops looking at it, and looks at him coming out of the kitchen with his sleeves wet to the elbow.
“Laney said if I didn’t bring it back she’d wear it to rush.” She holds the jacket out. He takes it. It’s warm from her arm.

body.text: “Tell your brother his jacket walked a girl home,” she says, quieter, just for him. He hangs it on the hook by the walk-in, where he can see it.
body.else: “It did three miles in the fog,” she says. “It’s earned a night off.” He hangs it on the hook by the walk-in, where he can see it.

body.text: There’s a weight in the inside pocket when he hangs it: the Reds, one short.
The Reds are still in the inside pocket when he hangs it, the pack exactly the way he left it at the end of the pier.
Then she takes his pack of Reds out of her cardigan pocket and sets it on the counter by the register and slides it across to him with one finger. “Held,” she says. “Every one. Count them.”

body: She takes a stool at the counter. Gloria comes down the counter with the coffee pot and stops in front of her and looks her over, top to bottom, the gray bun tilted, the pencil in it like a pin through a butterfly. “You walked out on me in August. Left a five on a two-dollar coffee.” Lena opens her mouth, all New Orleans manners, to apologize. “You’re the one he went after.” Gloria pours without looking at the cup. “Pecan,” she says. “Sweet all the way through, and it’ll break your teeth if you’re not careful.”

One of the fishermen laughs into his pie. Lena takes this in, and decides — he can watch her decide it — to be flattered. Then she sees the board by the register, the four still up there in chalk, and she pounces on it. “*Nine?* Costigan gave something a *nine*?” She swings round to the fishermen. “Y’all. Does the diocese know? Has anybody called Rome?” She turns back on the stool. “Ma’am, I’ll have whatever made Youngstown give out a nine.”

Gloria brings it. Lena eats it the way she does everything, all the way, and points her fork at him through the pass. “Eight. I’m taking one off for you being right.” And then, with a mouthful, dead serious: “WHO DAT. One day. Ten a.m., Sully’s. Black and gold or don’t come.” He doesn’t own anything black and gold, and she has to know it. She’s smiling at him like that’s his problem to solve, and it’s the first time all week the smile has been close enough to touch.

At 12:04 the LG goes off on the counter by her saucer. She looks at the screen, and something comes up in her face that has been missing since Monday, and she says, “Excuse me,” to Gloria, and takes it out through the front door onto the wharf. Midnight here. Two in the morning in New Orleans.

Jack goes back to the Hobart, because there are racks. Through the window over the machine he can see her at the railing under the sodium light, the harbor black behind her — one arm wrapped around herself, the phone at her ear, laughing. Then not laughing. Then laughing again. He sends a rack through, and the steam fogs the glass, and when it clears she’s still listening.

She comes back in at 12:19 with the phone folded in her hand and sits back down on the stool. Jack is drying his hands in the pass. “Wes,” she says. “He’s at a party. He wanted to tell me the Saints are going to win today.” She tucks a five under the saucer, square. “He sounded happy.”

choices.text: “Good. I’m glad.”
response: He means it, mostly, and she can see the mostly and lets him keep it. “Me too,” she says, and drinks her coffee.

choices.text: “Tell him a Browns fan says good luck. He’ll know it’s a curse.”
response: She laughs. “I am not carrying a hex across the Rockies, Costigan. Not this week.”

choices.text: Lift a wet hand from the pass. Go back to the racks.
response: He lifts a hand, wet to the wrist, and goes back to the machine. When the steam clears she has turned back to her coffee, both hands around the cup.

body: Gloria refills her coffee and, for once, doesn’t rate anything.

body.text: At 12:28 the last 11 shows its lights at the end of the wharf and she’s off the stool at a run, the cardigan flying. “Goodnight, Jack,” she calls from the door, and he’s back at the Hobart before the bell stops.

body: When he goes past the hook by the walk-in with a bus tub on his hip, the jacket smells of the harbor, and of the fog on Ocean Road, and faintly of somebody else’s shampoo. Rudy, without looking up, slides a plate of eggs onto the pass: dish man eats. Patsy Cline starts over. Jack sets the tub down by the Hobart and pulls the door, and the steam comes up.
